was as nothing to Adam's dazed state. "Listen, Adam," he said, "there is a legend about the diamond, a very old one. There was a beautiful princess who fell in love with the prince of Morocco. The prince promised to marry her back out of pity, but before the marriage could be settled the princess refused his hand and her lover seized the prince's hand and made her forget her own fears. She refused him with the promise that she would marry him, know his name, and bring him home to-morrow, but he was told that when he became so beautiful there would be no beauty left. Slave or free, the diamond was to him as the apple to a woman! But the prince was a faithful husband. With all his faults the diamond was pledged to him as a token that he would love him. He held the bargain and the two fell in love. And then—" "There was a terrible storm at sea," said Adam bitterly. "So I thought—so it was. It came over me that I was losing my mind. I was dreaming of a paradise beyond the mountains. I felt like a slave." There was a pause. Adam felt afraid to say his real name. He tried to remember how he had seen the beautiful princess and the beautiful boy that night. But his memory was strong and his heart beat strangely. He felt a wild longing to see the girl again. There was no other choice. With the fierce desire gone out of him he furtively kissed her and went away. But he longed to get away from her. "Leave my room," he said, suddenly, "or we shall both be murdered." Adam looked at her in bewilderment. What strange prophecy had warned him! He could not believe it of her! The sense of honor that Adam had given her had recurred upon him. Was this the way in which he had seen her? That she had hidden away her real self? But the thought came to him that this was indeed the case. The beautiful girl was lovely—doubly beautiful. It was the fashion she had worn when she first fell in love. And now that she was coming into the world she was very beautiful. The last time he had ever seen her she was so beautiful! But he was only able to say that she was beautiful because she was so beautiful. Love!—why could he not believe that this was the one? What could it be? Why
"I am the man I have always loved and always will love. And I will be frank with you: With this little woman I am different. I am a sensitive, beautiful creature, a beautiful woman, and love is dead." There was a little pause. Then Adam looked up, his eyes burning. "Margarita! You have forgotten me—you have forgotten me!" He touched the long, tender fingers dainty with true affection. "She is mine! But you must forgive me for the loneliness, the time when I am your wife. I would lie awake and never dreamt of you again. Margarita—if I only knew where she is!" The girl started up and touched him hard. "Margaret!" he answered unsteadily. "You do not know what you are doing. While I am lying here—never dreamt—for a moment—I kiss you—ma—kiss you—you kiss me! Yes, take this—this—this—ugly creature—eh, that's worse than the first! I cannot endure it any longer!" She laughed through him like a beast into the world. "But you are a beautiful girl!" she said. "You are only a little girl, but beautiful! I believe you are beautiful—but not as much as you think. You are a beautiful woman, but not the loveliest woman ever was. Is it any wonder that I hate you—when you are so beautiful?" And Adam laughed again, but said nothing. "Margaret," he continued, his voice shaking, "I am full of regret—oh, I have no hope! I am powerless. I will tear myself away from her, and that is all I can say!" And he rose to his feet. Margarita! He held her hand and pressed it to his heated lips. His breath came more quickly, his breathing became more rapid. His eyes grew bright, his lips touched hers as if of pain. It was as if he wished to speak to her. Adam watched as the dark, wild night came on. The little girl shook her head like an animal, and Adam laughed outright. The girl drew her apron to her eyes and patted Adam's arm affectionately as she leaned her head against his shoulder. The night was cold and dark. Both Adam and Adam had had a dream. That was the worst of sorrow. The two boys were destined to meet again. CHAPTER IX MARGARET

▶ offset=0 startsIt is pleasant to▶ offset=5 starts watch them; to be sure they are all half naked, but they have well-formed and healthy limbs▶ offset=25 starts, and their games are more childishly gay than any which I have ever seen other children play. This is the vulnerable spot of the horny Siegfried, who is here called Waldteufel. Smiling at the little ones under the larch-tree, I try after a while to mingle with them in their games, but they draw back shyly, only a few keeping near me; but when I attempt to get the better of them in a race or game of tag, then they all join in. And soon I am a good and welcome friend in the mad, whirling circle of these young people. I prattle many things to them, but more often I let them talk to me. I go to school to the children to learn the schoolmaster's art. The forest people do not allow themselves to be drawn up by force; he who would win them for higher things must descend quite to them, must lead them up arm in arm and indeed by a long, circuitous route. IN THE FELSENTHAL Below the slopes of the fore-alps and the cliffs of the Hochzahn with its chain of glaciers, the wooded hills extend on and on toward the west. Seen from above they lie there like a dark-blue sea, concealing in their depths the everlasting shadows and the strange people. A day's journey from the valley of the Winkel toward the west, far below the last hut, is a place where, according to the legend, the world is fastened in with boards. It were better said, walled in with stones; deep fissured precipices shut off the forest-land and here begin the Alps, where the rocky boulders no longer lie or lean, but soar straight up into the sky. A sea of snow and ice with crags, about which hover everlasting mists, extends endlessly, it is said, over the giant strongholds above, which in olden times guarded an Eden now turned to stone. Thus the legend. Strange that this wonderful dream of a lost paradise yet to be regained should dawn in the hearts of all people and nations! These foresters will not believe that on the other side of the Alps there are again regions inhabited by man. Only one old, shy, blinking charcoal-burner repeats the story told him by▼ offset=0 ends his grandfather, that over▼ offset=5 ends there were human beings, who wore such high pointed hats that they could not walk about on the mountains▼ offset=25 ends

In this mountain glen are a number of places held in ill repute. Here many a dead chamois-hunter has been found, shot through the breast by a ball of lead. There is also a legend that a monster, which keeps watch over an inexhaustible treasure of diamonds in the mountains, sometimes bursts forth from one of the numerous rocky caverns. If the forest-land endures a while longer, then a hero is expected to come and slay the beast and recover the treasure. Up to the present such a one has not appeared. Ah, if I could give this monster its true name! The region is adapted to the gloomy myths. It is a dead valley in which no little finch will sing, no wild pigeon coo, no woodpecker chatter, in which loneliness itself has fallen asleep. Upon the grey moss-covered ground piles of rock lie about, just as they have been broken from the high cliff. Here and there a bold little fir-tree has climbed up on one of these grey, weather-beaten boulders and proudly looks about, thinking itself now more fortunate than the other half-dead trees on the sandy soil below. It will not be long before it too will perish from hunger and thirst, and will fall from the barren rock. Here the forest cannot flourish, and if a straight and slender fir shoots up anywhere, its days are numbered. A storm-wind suddenly comes rushing down from the rocky defile and almost gently lays the young tree, together with its broken roots, upon the ground. The Scotch fir alone is still courageous; it climbs the steep sides between the precipices to discover how it looks up there with the Edelweiss, with the Alpine roses, with the chamois, and how far it is yet to the snow. But the good Scotch fir is no daughter of the Alps; soon a dizziness seizes it, and, frightened, it crouches down and crawls painfully upon its knees, with its twisted, crippled arms always reaching out and clutching something, the little heads of the cones stretching themselves upward in curiosity, until finally it comes out into the damp veil of mist and aimlessly wanders about among the stones.

the mountains of the Alps lie the regions of eternal snow. The Alpine mountains are not much like those of the Rhine and the Rhone, which, according to the legend, are inhabited by a race of people who claim to have no souls. They are said to have lived in caves, and were destroyed by the armies of the Tartars in the time of Christ. Now, it is said that the Alpine Germans, who live over against the Alps in this region, have learned to make use of the mountains for fire-works, and to build and plant new dams in the lakes of the Alps. They have a form of worship in which it is said that they can be seen drawing the beams and rafters of the rocks to the spot where the mountains stand. They still live on the mountains, but they have built great rock houses at the foot of the rocks, and built round towers, in which they build their great flimsy stone houses, the one tower being the tallest, and the others the lightest, as they call it. These dwellings are built of stone, and in some places the ground is well drained and sloped down to the bare rock beneath. The entrance to this form of dwelling is a broad and lofty one, a door in the rock being hardly more than a few inches high and too small to admit of a rude carvings-table, a little box, or a little pulpit. A stair, too, is yet seen at the top, and at the head of this stair is the priest's skull, as he stands near the entrance which leads into the sacred mysteries of this mountain church. The steep rock overhangs the little river which flows through the valley of the Winkel, and the mountain stream becomes suddenly visible at night, when the hollow hills, clothed in larch, are found around the edge of the valley. The mountain church, with its tapering roof, is one of the most ancient and beautiful sights in this region. ▶ offset=0 startsAnd there were walls▶ offset=5 starts sculptured with deep indentations and long passages that crept away from the light. Altogether▶ offset=25 starts it was a very weird and awe-inspiring place, and as a general thing one did not feel like making much noise in it, especially since there were so many echoes to disturb. "Everything seems to be just where we left it since the night we hazed Bull Harris here," laughed Mark. "Poor Bull was about scared blue that day." "An' thar's the shovel the Parson dug his treasure with," chuckled Texas. "What air we agoin' to do now?" "Bury these clothes for the first thing," was the answer. "Then I can breathe freely again." This task was soon accomplished, and then Mark sat down in one of the chairs—​for the counterfeiters had furnished their cave. "I'm thinking," observed Mark, meditatively, "that we might have a good deal of fun exploring all the passages and dark places in this cave. Who knows what we might find?" "Whoop!" cried Texas, springing up in excitement. "Sho' enough! We might find a new entrance!" "Yes, and we might find some deuced pitfalls, ye know, bah Jove!" observed Chauncey. "Or bears, b'gee!" chuckled Dewey. "Oo! oo!" gasped poor Indian. "Don't talk that way, please. Bless my soul, I know I shall drop dead with fright." At that same instant something happened so unexpected and so horrible that it struck them motionless and chill. A deep low groan, as if of agony, echoed through the lonely cave! For a moment the Seven glanced at each other in consternation and dread. They were almost paralyzed by the sound, which had evidently come from one of the inner recesses of the cavern. Poor Indian had sunk down on the ground in a heap. "What's that?" they cried, and then listened. But the groan was not repeated. They waited in fear and trembling, but the rocks gave not another sound, and suddenly Mark sprang to his feet. "Fellows," he cried, "there's somebody in here! Who'll follow me?" To tell the truth, they were all very much afraid and were not at all successful in hiding it. The sound had been so weird and horrible. terrified as any of them, but he shook it off with a desperate effort and sprang into the air. "Wow! hooray!" he cried, "here comes another!" The cave was a large one, and the five friends had everything in common. They paused in the darkness to watch the Visitors, and from this different place they could faint a little from the fearful hordes of darkness and suspense that swept through the world as the Evening Eyes closed upon them. And now they were stationed at the entrance and fastened to the cave wall, with the exception of the Indian who had hidden the leaden missiles and carried them back to the cave. The Five were too weak to attempt anything save to get in under the cover of the dark cave, where they would not be discovered. They had picked up some of the cinders that stood on the table, which the Five had seen fit to scatter in the darkness, and so forth, and they were filling up the darkness with strange unearthly sounds that decided the moment to make another effort and get away. "Now," whispered Mark, "breakfast soon. We've got so many things to talk over, that's jist the nicest talk we've ever all heard. Pretty soon we'll be close up, and then—" He did not finish the sentence. But he did not wait to inquire. He was convinced that they were just going to put in a fresh supply of cartridges and bullets, and that they would be all ready to start. "O!" cried the Five, as soon as they were sure that they had really started upon the next step. "We'll be up against it pretty hard, if we don't bring up an extra set." They pushed away the cartridges that were piled high in front of the cave door, and began to descend the rock, pushing it away from the cave. When they reached the entrance they found that the Five had gone out and were resting. "Stand up!" bellowed Texas, and then they could hear him whispering:— "Over there, too, at the entrance!" Mark was now hurrying back toward the entrance and they could hear plainly enough that he was afraid the Five would go up past them. He would hardly have been able to get down again, however, had they obeyed the Five's promptings. Their bullets would have done the work, for they would have known that one
about him. "What's that in your ear?" he shouted, and tried to conceal his excitement, but it was useless. "It's you," he gasped, "I—er I know you—" "No, no!" cried the Indian. "What's that?" They seemed about to crash in the cavern, and Mark, in a frenzy of joy, drew forth the boundless handful of gold, showing that he was the same old Sam Houston, who had come to this portion of Texas in a canoe. Mark saw that the Indians had all fled, and he knew that they did not mean to remain in the cave long enough to be rescued. Mark was silent a while; but a quick glance at the group could not have given him a more vivid idea of what was going on. He had made up his mind that the old cave was the only hiding place in that part of Texas. He had come to this place to hunt for his little boy, and he had told him that he was going to make a search there until he was ready to return. "I don't know what you mean by 'here'—'there's a cave under my house,' as I was watching, but it's been shut up, and I've been looking all around for you." "Yes, I saw it," nodded Sam, and he was good at guesswork, which is always a good sign. "No," explained Sam, "she didn't find my cave, and so she left me to alone. I guess it was all right, and I've been on a lot of treasure hunt all day." "Nonsense!" grunted Sam. "I'm glad you don't believe it." "Well, I didn't mean to believe it, but you got my meaning, and I guess you're right," smiled Sam. "If you ever do," echoed the old man, hastily, "don't say that. I know what you mean." "Well, then," said Sam, rising, "I'll never believe it. You may as well understand that now, and for the future, we'll have a try." Mark looked at the old man curiously, and spoke in his ear, of the beauty of the night, and he laughed and shook his head. "We don't know that you have it all to yourself," he said. ▶ offset=0 startsNunky kindly brought▶ offset=5 starts him some sarsaparilla-mead, wondering what would be wanted next. "More▶ offset=25 starts pictures, Nunky: I mean, please!" Nunky brought another beautiful painting, which he placed against the foot-board of the bed. "Oh! Jesus talking to the woman. Isn't it splendid? Did he always look so sober, Nunky?" "No, I presume not." "Well, I don't fink he did, 'cept when little children were naughty, or Jerusalem got out of order," remarked Pollio, glancing at an engraving on the wall called "Christ weeping over Jerusalem." Of course Jerusalem must have "got out of order," or he would not have wept over it. Pollio moved his head on the pillow uneasily. He remembered that he, too, had "got out of order;" and he did not like to look at that beautiful, sad face at the foot of the bed, for it seemed to know and feel sorry he had been so naughty. "Wish you'd take that picture away, please!" said Pollio, twisting his mouth as if in pain. "Why, what's the matter, General?" "Wish I'd runned away! Wish I had runned away!" groaned the child, in such a tone of anguish that Nunky began to fear he was losing his reason. "Wish you'd runned away? Why, I should think you'd had trouble enough for one day, without wishing for more." "Wish I'd runned away from the 'Finny-castics'—there! They kep' a-comin', and I kep' a-stayin'. That's why I got stepped on, 'cause I kep' a-stayin'." "Yes, I don't doubt you are right, General: if you had not staid, you would not have been stepped on. But how did you happen to be in the street?" "I was hunting for the disappearance of my lost b'loon," said Pollio, who still used large words in the wrong place sometimes. "Well, did you find the disappearance?" "Yes, sir. But 'twas all busted up, sticking on the fence; and I lost it again. Oh, dear! I ought to not gone, and I ought to not staid, and▼ offset=0 ends I ought to not—▼ offset=5 endswhere's mamma?" "Asleep, I hope. What do you want of her?" ▼ offset=25 ends

That's a very good question to ask. And here she comes," said Nunky, slipping out of the room; for he had waited upon cross Pollio for four hours, and needed rest. Pollio confessed his naughtiness, and his mother forgave him at once. Did you ever hear of a mother that wouldn't forgive her darling child? "O mamma! I sha'n't ever do anyfing bad any more," said Pollio, laying his little brown cheek against hers, so glad his sins were over for life. "I felt awful bad, and that was why I wanted that water and that cream beer; but it didn't do me any good. But now—O mamma!" "What, dear?" "If I only had some lemonade!" "But I dare not give it to you, my child. Won't you try to be happy without it?" "Yes, mamma," sighed Pollio. "I'll be happy if I can see my Posy. But, if I don't see her pretty soon, I'm afraid I'll die!" This touched his mother's heart, and she called Nunky to send for Posy. The little girl entered the room with a look of the deepest grief on her little face; but Pollio said bravely, as Nunky lifted her up to kiss him,— "Poh, I'd twice as rather get hurt than have you, Posy! I'm a boy!" Posy's only answer was to stroke his cheek softly, and sob. "That wolf stepped on me, that's all. Don't cry, Posy! No, 'twas Billy Barstow—I mean the colt." "Naughty fing! I don't like Fourfs of July!" said the gentle sister, not quite sure whether to blame the colt, the wolf, or Billy. "O Nunky! won't you set her up on the bed side o' me?" said Pollio, who found her remarks very consoling. "I've lost my b'loon Posy: where's yours?" "Well, I didn't lost mine: a hole came into it." ▶ offset=0 startsMeanwhile, I sew▶ offset=5 starts and sew at that eternal Embroidery, or try to keep myself awake with a Book, if▶ offset=25 starts I can find one to my Mind, till my Lady returns jaded or excited from the Ridotto, to be undressed and have hot Soup in Bed. Thus, you see, I have no Change, no Exercise; and what is worse, no Food or Medicine for the Mind; and oh, Patty! is this a Life for an accountable Creature?" Illustration Chapter VII. Lady Betty's Fright. "However that may be, Gatty," said I, "'tis certain you and I have not the Power of rectifying Abuses, and must take Things as we find them; but you must console yourself with thinking your Trial will probably not be long, for I'll wager a Pound you'll be married within the Twelvemonth." "Who to?" says she, opening her Eyes wide. "Nay, I can't tell that," said I, "but you are not the Sort of Girl to be overlooked." She smiled sadly and said, "You are only speaking at Random, nor have I any Wish to be married, any further than I should like almost any Condition better than my own. But now, tell me, Patty, is it not a bad State of Things when young Women are so placed as that they are tempted to look to Marriage as an Escape?" "Certainly it is," said I; "but yet, Gatty, let me tell you, your Condition might be many Degrees worse than it now is. Nay, if you had been born and bred to Servitude, you might even consider you had a tolerable Place; 'tis your gentler Birth and Bringing-up that makes the Collar so hard to wear. Suppose, for Instance, Lady Betty, in addition to her Caprice and Frivolity, had the Sufferings, Infirmities, and confirmed Ill-Humours of old Age? Or suppose she were married to a troublesome Husband? Or, even as she is, that she were a Martyr to some irritating Complaint?" "Then I would nurse her with Pity and Patience," says Gatty. "However, 'tis no use supposing this and the other—I must take my Lot and make the best of it; only I sometimes envy the Shop-Girls behind the poorest Counter, for methinks they have more Exercise and Variety,▼ offset=0 ends and have at least their▼ offset=5 ends Sundays to themselves; whereas, 'e'en Sunday shines no Sabbath-Day to me.'" After Breakfast, Mr. James the Footman made his Appearance in Undress Livery, carrying a small Trunk, and requested to see Mrs. Gatty. When she appeared, "Mrs. Gatty," says he—"dear me, how you've fallen away! you must have been ill indeed!... I was about to say, your Billet to my Lady threw us into sad Confusion Yesterday. I carried it to her on a Salver, and she, not knowing who sent it, opened it carelessly, when, seeing your Name, she dropped it like a red-hot Coal, and fell back on her Settee, crying to me to throw the Billet in the Fire. But then called me back to bid me look in it first, and see what you said, she smelling to her Scent-Bottle all the While. When I told her Ladyship the Contents, she said she would by no Means have you back yet, it would be highly dangerous, and perhaps cost many precious Lives; that you had better go down somewhere into the Country, to your Home, in short, till you got thoroughly disinfected; and after that she would let you know her Mind about you. So I have brought your Trunk, and your Half-Year's Wages; and here are five Pounds to clear off your Expenses here and pay for your Journey into the Country." I never saw a Face light up with Joy as Gatty's did, that Moment! "Oh, this is delightful!" said she, "Thank you kindly, James, for being the Bearer of such good Tidings! I have little Doubt that I shall be quite strong and well after spending a Month at Home, and then I will do as my Lady pleases." When the Man was gone, she pressed the five Pounds on my Mother, with the humblest Expressions of Gratitude; but my Mother would by no Means take it. "I hope she will prove an Enjoyment to you, dear Lady Betty, ever since you have been so good and so good," said I, "and beamingly kind to you at Sex." "It seems to suit my Feelings most," says he, "to your Grace's very Gracious Heart." "If you find me in such an Improvidence," says he, "I shall be obliged to turn up at Court, and place myself under the Care of an experienced Friend." "Poor woman," said Lady Betty, looking very pretty, "she has had a bad Triage; but her Admissions are all done with a Speed. She seems to enjoy it, and hopes for a good Time at least with her Husband." "Her Practice is good," says I; "but it will be very good Practice, Gatty." "Most Gatty Women are either Church-Women, or Men. Neither is likely to be so," said I; "but, on the contrary, it will be well for them that you should be, or that they will make a better Man than is generally the case." "For Instance? What do you mean?" said I. "I mean, most happily," said Gatty. "You should be very good Nurses, Gatty. I should not be very good at all." "Very well, Gatty," said I; "but if Religion makes you unfit, or discouraged, you must be sensible, I hope, of believing in a Place out to Stay, and keeping it open, every Day. I should like to see the Shop-Girl's still better and quicker Methods, and the more inwards than the Shop-Girls. This Plan I have had on Spot it; but it is only delayin' itself. Goodness knows when I shall be better suited to take it than when I am. So, Gatty, I must try that." "You must be Satisfied then," said I, "if I catch the Hugger without the Hugger." This is only a Design, to keep her out of the Shop-Girls' Circle, and give the Shop-Girls a Home." "What
Word on my Lips as to what the Shop-Women might have to say on the subject of their Shop-Women; but it seems there is a palpable tinge in their Affections that attracts not only Eyes, but a certain Humour to the Dark. "The same Sense of Humour plays on me," says I, "you will find nothing against it, I hope; but then, though I am a very sensible Man, and take Pleasure at having the Sense of our Hearts, I was not till after I had tried to marry you, as I was going to say; and this I have often observed in young Women—By their Nurturing, their Love, and their Fear of Pregnancy; and though I cannot but think that Nature is not only more Affectionate to them than Art or Law or Money, yet she has more Pride or Self-Conceit in her Husband than in any other Woman, and I suspect she would not Rate herself if she were but a Common Labourer. Now I am sure you would not have more Sense of Humour in this Country, especially when you can form a juster Judgment of Women, if you had no Sense of Humour in your Mind, and no buttress in your Hearts; for only the heavier Women are apt to be Humoured, and often it is to their Judgment that they are over-comed. I cannot but think the hard, old-fashioned Sense of Humour in Women, is much too much at variance with the refined Sensitivity of the Sex. Women are too sensible to know that there is such a Thing as Humour, when once indulged in, and that the Sensitivity of Women is a Thing of the Past, when they have been taught to look upon it as a Thing utterly repugnant to their male Self. I believe there is a Humour in Woman which makes her the less Humourous of all, and I would not know how to account for it, except in a System of Comparative Humour. And yet, withal, it is a delicate, ill-timed Humour that makes the Pleasure or Pain of Women so great. Yet, there is no lack of Humour in Woman, if there is any; and I must confess that I have sometimes rather too much Humour in my Heart. And I must confess that I sometimes think myself very silly, if I am really a fool. And yet, Patty, I have been thinking of you

▶ offset=0 starts"Commissioner Shield▶ offset=5 starts had in 1810, with that humanity and judgment for which he was remarkable, suggested to the▶ offset=25 starts Navy Board, that the negroes employed in the dock-yard should be put on the same footing as landsmen on board His Majesty's ships, having the same allowance of provision, and the same pay; the latter amounting to £14 per annum, the balance of which after the deduction made for their clothes (as in the case of seamen) should be carried to their credit, and kept until they were out of their time, as a means of future provision. After the departure of Commissioner Shield this salutary arrangement had been lost sight of, in consequence of which Sir Jahleel Brenton wrote the following letter to the Navy Board; which as it describes the useful services of these men, and led to advantageous results in their behalf, it may not be amiss to introduce. " Simon's Bay, 31st May, 1815. " Gentlemen, "I beg leave to lay before you an account of the black men now belonging to this establishment, with a few observations respecting them. "By your letter to Commissioner Shield, 13th September, 1810, you were pleased to approve of his suggestions of these black people being borne as landsmen, and those who had acquired the ability to work as caulkers being allowed such further encouragement as he thought proper. Accordingly the men then in the yard were so regulated; but those who arrived subsequently to that period have only been put upon the footing of boys of the third class, and continued as such till the time of my arrival here. Upon enquiry I have found that the labour of this latter description is equally valuable and hard with that of the former, and I in consequence directed them to be put on the same footing, and submit to you the propriety of their being allowed the arrears of pay which would have been their due, had they received the benefit of your order on their first arrival. "It was I believe the intention of Commissioner Shield to have given them that advantage, had they arrived from Plettenburg Bay, previous to his departure from this country; they were all grown men upon their first arrival. "Several of the most intelligent of the black men have been placed under the direction of the different artificers, and some by assiduity and good conduct have acquired such a degree of skill in their craft▼ offset=0 ends, as to enable His▼ offset=5 ends Majesty's service to derive a considerable benefit from their work. "I have thought it my duty▼ offset=25 ends
▼ offset=0 starts, as to enable His▼ offset=5 starts Majesty's service to derive a considerable benefit from their work. "I have thought it my duty▼ offset=25 starts to extend to these the indulgence granted by Commissioner Shield to the caulkers, viz. ordinary seamen's pay, which I hope you will approve of, as it will be a spur to their companions.... "By their assistance the buildings (in the dock-yard, &c.) will be erected at much less expense than by any other mode of procuring labourers. They have the benefit of the school, and I am sanguine in the hope of their deriving great benefit from it. "As I am upon the subject of the negroes, I must request your indulgence to a few remarks which a daily observation of their situation, docility and general usefulness, constantly suggests to me. "These unfortunate people at the period of their arrival in the colony are in general from twenty to thirty years of age, many of them older, and by the present regulations of Government, they are to serve fourteen years, before they can obtain their freedom. "The negroes seldom attain an advanced age, the generality of them are past their strength at a much earlier period than the white people, and consequently at the end of their servitude, may have no other prospect than a helpless old age before them, at a time when they must depend upon their own labour for their support. "I am aware that their servitude can only be shortened by the interference of His Majesty's ministers; but my object in addressing you upon the subject is, that you would be pleased to take the case into consideration, and to allow such as are really valuable to Government in different branches, to receive an allowance bearing some proportion to their earnings. I should say, half-a crown a day, including their provisions. "I should not allow this indulgence to be extended to them without long and ample experience of its being duly earned, to be certified by the respective officers. By these means a provision might be laid up for them, and so much energy exerted as to produce the most salutary results. "Many of the blacks have made a considerable progress in learning, but those landed from the ships are only beginning. "I have, &c. "J. BRENTON." " To Navy Board. "I am aware of the necessity which exists for every improvement of the other race, and many tender convictions already hinted that it is necessary to increase this year; but with a full knowledge of what is at present required of the black men, is every day more of interest to them and less complained of in other branches of the service. "One thing to be thought of, in this case, is, that these poor men's allowances may not be superseded even by an increase of wages; there are other ways yet open to them of obtaining a income out of somewhat less than the sum of six figures paid annually by the Navy Company on their passage to America. "In some cases the wages seem to me very moderate, although the late increases of wages were very slight, owing to the prohibitive duties which had been imposed on them by their former masters. In the course of normal conditions they are liable to be drawn into slavery, or some similar evil termed dirt, rather than to remain long in a place. The contract for the repair of these walls would cost them about 15s. to 18s. sterling; yet I have conceived there could be 30,000 whites à lati on the same ground in a year, and even if I am justified in the sums received, their labour would still produce 100,000 worth of work in central Africa, where many of them are already engaged. I grant the proposition as it lies between me and the best men, but I do not conceive it to be so in the light of my own experience. "I delay until the erection of the barracks, in carrying out which vessels, etc., may be lodged, or else I should happen to stop on Ontario Street, somewhere about the neighbourhood of this address. The accommodation of bridges is doubtless sometimes met with in this country; but I shall find it difficult to secure sufficient accommodation for 2000 men each day. The reserve at the station of St. Omer is extensive, and will undoubtedly be very valuable. "An hour's support afforded me for my work I am rather inclined to prefer, as the home of civilisation in general is preferable to the private station, where comfort is always considered the first requisite. ▶ offset=0 startsThe certificate of stock▶ offset=5 starts was in the safe keeping of Amasa Culpepper, who had given a receipt for the same▶ offset=25 starts, and a promise to hand over the original certificate when this paper was produced." "And you say the receipt disappeared from the table in your sitting room, without anybody knowing what became of it?" asked Tom. "Yes," replied Carl. "This is how it came about. Lately we received word that the company had struck some gushers in the way of wells, and that the stock my father had bought for a few cents a share is worth a mint of money now. It was through Amasa Culpepper my mother first learned about this, and she wrote to the company to find out." "Oh! I see," chuckled Tom, "and when Mr. Culpepper learned that there was a chance of your mother becoming rich, his unwelcome attentions became more pronounced than ever; isn't that so, Carl?" "I think you're right, Tom," said the other boy, but without smiling, for he carried too heavy a load on his mind to feel merry. "You see my mother had hunted up this precious receipt, and had it handy, meaning to go over to Mr. Culpepper's office in the forenoon and ask for the certificate of stock he has in his safe." "So she laid it on the table, did she?" pursued Tom, shaking his head. "Don't you think that it was a little careless, Carl, in your mother, to do that?" "She can't forgive herself for doing it," replied his chum, sadly. "She says that it just shows how few women have any business qualities about them, and that she misses my father more and more every day that she lives. But none of the other children touched the paper. Angus, Elsie and Dot have told her so straight; and it's a puzzle to know what did become of it." "You spoke of hunting in the garden and around the outside of the house; why should you do that?" "It happened that one of the sitting room windows was open half a foot that day. The weather had grown mild you remember," explained the other. "And you kind of had an idea the paper might have blown out through that open window, was that it?" "It looked like it to me," answered the widow's son, frowning; "but if that was what happened the wind carried it over the fence and far away, because I▼ offset=0 ends've not been able to▼ offset=5 ends find anything of it." "How long was it between the time your mother laid the paper on the table▼ offset=25 ends
▼ offset=0 starts've not been able to▼ offset=5 starts find anything of it." "How long was it between the time your mother laid the paper on the table▼ offset=25 starts and the moment she missed it?" continued Tom Chesney. "Just one full hour. She went from the breakfast table and got the paper out of her trunk. Then when she had seen the children off to school, and dressed to go out it was gone. She said that was just a quarter to ten." "She's sure of that, is she?" demanded Tom. "Yes," replied Carl, "because the grocer's boy always comes along at just a quarter after nine for his orders, and he had been gone more than twenty minutes." At that the other boy stopped still and looked fixedly at Carl. "That grocer's boy is a fellow by the name of Dock Phillips, isn't he?" was what Tom asked, as though with a purpose. "Yes," Carl replied. "And he works for Mr. Amasa Culpepper, too!" continued Tom, placing such a decided emphasis on these words that his companion started and stared in his face. "That's all true enough, Tom, but tell me what you mean by saying that in the way you did? What could Mr. Culpepper have to do with the vanishing of that paper?" "Oh! perhaps nothing at all," pursued the other, "but all the same he has more interest in its disappearance than any other person I can think of just now." "Because his name was signed at the bottom, you mean, Tom?" cried the startled Carl. "Just what it was," continued Tom. "Suppose your mother could never produce that receipt, Mr. Culpepper would be under no necessity of handing over any papers. I don't pretend to know much about such things, and so I can't tell just how he could profit by holding them. But even if he couldn't get them made over in his own name, he might keep your mother from becoming rich unless she agreed to marry him!" Carl was so taken aback by this bold statement that he lost his breath for a brief period of time. "But Tom, Amasa Culpepper wasn't in our house that morning?" he objected. "Perhaps not, but Dock Phillips was, and he's a boy I'd hate to trust any further than I could see him," Tom agreed. "Do you think Mr. Culpepper could have hired Dock to steal the paper?" continued the sorely-puzzled Carl. "Well, hardly that. If Dock took it he did the job on his own responsibility. find anything of it." "How long was it between the time your mother laid the paper on the table so many years ago, and the time when the window was opened?" asked Tom, with interest. "About three months ago. The morning I called and found it was unopened, and downright chilly. I gave orders to the servants to get the stove and brush, and found they had the room." "Oh! it's all the same, excepting here; I only came out for a bit of a stroll once in awhile, and the first thing I knew was the fire was out, showing the door of the room!" cried Carl, with a shudder. "Is this it, Tom?" asked Tom, with much curiosity. "Yes, it was, just this through the window; that's how it happened." "Come on," cried Tom, seizing his chisel tip from the ground. "We don't mean to miss the chance, do we?" "Oh! I don't suppose it did," replied Tom, smiling. "We must have been mistaken!" "The window crack, Carl. All the hinges were sound. I don't think it would have done so well in this house as it did half an hour ago. You ought to have wished for a safe just large enough for a place at the end. I expect it would have been open all the way round, with wide one heels and a door above it. I never saw it look so badly in my house as it did when we put it up last spring." "What! The inside of that window crack; that would be too much for us. I don't see how you could feel about it for fear we should open it again. If she was all right, they'd have the window open; and we could all get in and out and slip in." "But it will never do to open the window," said Tom, with a grim laugh. "Why should it; how could we open it?" asked Tom, with mischievous levity. "Thank you, but don't you see, Carl, it's a guarantee of this house that we don't have to open it again. Besides, it's not locked as you notice; it just isn't." "How glad I was that it didn't!" cried Tom, with amazement, for there was no answer in sight. "Oh! not very likely it would have been any better if they hadn't," answered the widow. "But the bolts
in your sitting room and the time when you saw the paper lying on the table?" asked Carl. "About two years before she married my father; and after she went away, she was called down for a week or two every summer, to go to school and learn to read and write. I suppose she read to her mother and the rest of the family all the time?" "Oh! she was only a child," remarked Tom. "But she didn't say much about her mother's marriage; and I guess she didn't have any choice." "She was engaged to some one else, I suppose," admitted the other, with a meaning look at the gloomy frown on his face. "I hope that happened," Tom continued. "She had a little brother who was very fond of her brother, and I believe she was just as sweet and good as she could be." "Pretty nice little girl, too," said Tom, brightening a little. "Oh! she didn't say she was your mother, I suppose," said Tom, with a smile that was almost half forced; "but she was a pretty nice baby, and I think she was a mean old thing." "He wasn't a mean old thing," spoke Tom, trying to show that he was pleased with the girl. "Well, I can see that she had a good deal of slang about her mother, and that she was very well and friendly. She was a pretty girl, too, and I've met her once or twice before I was in New York." "She was a pretty nice little girl," Tom continued, "but she didn't mean anything by her words, just all at once. She was a nice old woman, and she was very kind to me, and I was kind of like her mother, and she was very nice. And I wish you'd got a dictionary and a book and a subscription to the library, and I guess you'd be surprised to know how much I used to like reading when I was a boy." "I hope you didn't think there was any use in saying that to her, or anybody else," said Tom, drawing out a key from his pocket. "I know just what you mean, and if you're kind enough to open it you'll like me a lot. I don't mind a bit, though I suppose it's for her good. I don't think she likes me at all, and I don't think I should like to have my mother marry her

▶ offset=0 starts1894) shows▶ offset=5 starts greater similarity with Thrincoma. Thrinax praeceps sp. nov. Tr▶ offset=25 startsunk 8–12 cm. in diameter at base, columnar or slightly enlarged upward, seldom attaining over 3 or 4 meters in height. The leaf-bases split in the middle of the midrib and long remain adherent to the trunk. When they finally fall away on older trees a rather rough grayish and longitudinally chinked rimose surface is exposed. The stalks of large leaves measure 75–80 cm. in length and 1.2–1.5 cm. in width. The middle divisions of the leaf are 55 cm. and under in length and attain a width of 4.8 cm., and in the middle of large leaves are united for more than half their length. Cross-veinules numerous, distinct in both surfaces but especially the upper. The white pubescence or tomentum which clothes the young leaves and is especially abundant on the ligule soon disappears, leaving the under side glaucous or slightly pruinose. This species is described at some length a little later in a comparison of generic characters under Thrincoma alta. The type specimen (no. 850) was collected on the precipitous mountain-side which overhangs the road between Utuado and Arecibo, a short distance to the northward from the station where Thrincoma alta was obtained. What is believed to be the same species was collected in a similar situation on the side of a mountain overlooking the town and valley of Lares. Thrinax Ponceana sp. nov. Plate 43 Trunk 5–8 cm. or more in diameter, columnar, or slightly tapering or enlarged upward, 1–4 m. high; surface coarsely and irregularly rimose longitudinally. Leaf-bases separating into abundant rather loose light grayish or brownish fibers. Leaves numerous, large, drooping or pendant; petioles 65 mm. long, 1.5–2 cm. wide; segments attaining 75 cm. in length and 3.5 cm. in width, united for half their length. Seed smooth, mahogany-brown, 5 mm. in diameter. Type specimen no. 1005. This species apparently exists in much larger quantities than any other yet known from Puerto Rico, being the predominant▼ offset=0 ends plant on several square miles▼ offset=5 ends of territory along the range of dry limestone hills which skirt the southern coast of the island, to the▼ offset=25 ends
▼ offset=0 starts plant on several square miles▼ offset=5 starts of territory along the range of dry limestone hills which skirt the southern coast of the island, to the▼ offset=25 starts west of Ponce. Many of the palms are scattered among the taller shrubs and trees wherever there is sufficient soil and water to permit these to grow and yet not enough to give them exclusive possession, but on many of the drier and more sterile higher slopes the advantage is with the palms. This abundance of living material deserves more careful study than could be given during a very brief visit to this almost uninhabited part of the island, but one note of systematic interest was made. Several species of Thrinax, of which T. Morrisii Wendland may serve as an example, have been described chiefly with reference to the relative size of the leaf segments and the extent of their separation. If the palms under observation near Ponce belonged, as was believed, all to one species, it is not only true that the individual Thrinax passes all the stages from the narrow and grass-like, almost completely separated segments of the very young plant, to the more than half united leaf of the large tree, but it also appears to be true that under unfavorable conditions a Thrinax may not be able to attain to full maturity of size and form but may at the same time produce flowers and seeds. In the narrow chinks and crevices of the bare rocks were very small, stunted trees, obviously of great age, while but a few feet distant a deeper fissure might hold vegetable débris and moisture sufficient to nourish vigorous specimens several times the size of their less fortunate companions. The stunted trees retain in proportion to their size, but apparently with little reference to their age, the small deeply divided leaves of young plants and have short few-branched inflorescences, another difference of supposed systematic importance. In Thrinax Ponceana the leaves of well grown trees have the middle divisions united to about the middle; the smaller the leaves, the more deeply they are divided. A further correlation with size is that of the "fullness" of the leaf. The basal sinus is not closed by the overlapping of the lateral divisions as in some species, but the area is too great for a plane circle and there are one or more folds, more numerous and deeper in large leaves. The lateral divisions do not lie in the plane of the others but project upward or backward nearly at right angles with the plane of the middle divisions. Morrisii Wendland may serve as an example, have been described chiefly with reference to the relative size of the leaf segments and the extent of their separation. If the palms under observation near Ponce belonged, as was believed, all to one species, it is not only true that the individual Thrinax passes all the stages from the narrow and grass-like, almost completely separated segments of the very young plant, to the more than half united leaf of the large tree, but it also appears to be true that under unfavorable conditions a Thrinax may not be able to attain to full maturity of size and form but may at the same time produce flowers and seeds. In the narrow chinks and crevices of the bare rocks were very small, stunted trees, obviously of great age, while but a few feet distant a deeper fissure might hold vegetable débris and moisture sufficient to nourish vigorous specimens several times the size of their less fortunate companions. The stunted trees retain in proportion to their size, but apparently with little reference to their age, the small deeply divided leaves of young plants and have short few-branched inflorescences, another difference of supposed systematic importance. In Thrinax Ponceana the leaves of well grown trees have the middle divisions united to about the middle; the smaller the leaves, the more deeply they are divided. A further correlation with size is that of the "fullness" of the leaf. The basal sinus is not closed by the overlapping of the lateral divisions as in some species, but the area is too great for a plane circle and there are one or more folds, more numerous and deeper in large leaves. The lateral divisions do not lie in the plane of the others but project upward or backward nearly at right angles with the plane of the middle divisions. The middle

Many of the palms are scattered among the taller shrubs and trees wherever there is sufficient soil and water to permit these to grow and yet not enough to give them exclusive possession, but on many of the drier and more sterile higher slopes the advantage is with the palms. This abundance of living material deserves more careful study than could be given during a very brief visit to this almost uninhabited part of the island, but one note of systematic interest was made. Now, there is no need to retrospect us upon a possible hybridization between Thrinax and Thrinax, or any other closely related species as models for study of separation in Thrinax. Tiumano has been one of the most extensive and remote of natural habitats in the Puerto Rico Coast and Archipelago for decades, yet we have only seen a few of it in a broader light. As a matter of fact, plants of this genus remain scarce and critically to be sought for in the extreme western coasts of the United States. They are rather scarce and widely distributed in Tierra del Fuego, one of the most southern of the Californian islands, and only coming to light near the top of that overlying and underlying rocks, when an isolated wreck, seemingly uninhabitable by the die-off processes of time, is found below our feet in the apparently impenetrable mantle of the mountains. Tiumano has been recognized by the United States Department of Agriculture as a variety of Thrincoma "asinica," and is now classified under the genus Thrinax in the order Magnplocera. The species grows
west of Ponce. The leaves have a characteristic fragrance, rather like that of mature leaves of Thrinax Ponceana, and the young leaves of young plants are covered with a dense growth of white or grayish down. Thrinax Ponceana is of interest in the way it presents a single point of origin for the plants growing on its flat and fertile slopes. The bark of the younger trees is in some respects similar to that of Thrinax Ponceana, but is less thick, and certainly not as showy as most of the other species. The leaves are larger than those of Thrinax Ponceana, and are up to 80 cm. long and 25 cm. wide near the base, with a smooth surface; the apex is pointed and of a silvery white; the lateral veins extending back from the base are clothed in a greyish or brownish gray. The flower-heads are usually purplish, but a habit so gentle and charming as to attract attention must be reckoned as a preliminary consideration when one is in the position of desiring to establish a permanent colony of elderberry on Ponce. In addition to the length and breadth of the island there are indications that a change in this respect would soon have been effected in this region of Lares. The stem of the elder is covered with short and thick foliage. The stems are up to 12 cm. in diameter, with a thickened border; the leaves are smaller and lighter green on the upper side, and are here much shorter and finer. The flowers are rather scanty on this side of the island, but numerous in quantity. They are rather striking and varied in color. The corolla, however, is not as richly marked as that of Thrinax Ponceana. The same kind of plant is included in the series of native productions which have been described from time to time in Puerto Rico; such specimens are remarkably abundant 8 cm. in length and 2.5 cm. in breadth in the oldest ones, but most singular and striking in appearance. The leaves are usually clothed in a soft dull green veining on the outside edges of the leaves, the other veins being red. A few minute lines beyond the end of the leaf are seen showing the intense green of the leaf-bases and the thick blackish or grayish brown lines which are characteristic of the group of trees called gnetum.
